TOPIC 1, SUBTOPIC C: THE CIRCULATORY SYSTEM (Grade 7)

OBJECTIVES
Learners should be able to:
- name the main parts of the circulatory system
- describe the structure and function of the heart
- distinguish between arteries, veins and capillaries
- explain how exercise affects the heart and circulation
- relate a healthy circulatory system to sports performance

WHAT IS CIRCULATION?
Circulation is the continuous movement of blood around the body, driven by the heart. The circulatory system delivers oxygen (from the lungs) and nutrients (from digested food) to every cell in the body, while carrying away waste products such as carbon dioxide and urea to be removed.

THE HEART
The heart is a hollow, muscular organ about the size of a closed fist, located in the chest slightly to the left of the centre, protected by the ribcage. It is made of a special type of muscle called cardiac muscle, which never gets tired and contracts continuously throughout life without conscious control.
- Chambers: the heart has four chambers - two upper chambers called atria (singular: atrium) and two lower, more muscular chambers called ventricles. The right side of the heart deals with deoxygenated blood, while the left side deals with oxygenated blood; a muscular wall called the septum keeps the two sides separate.
- Valves: one-way valves inside the heart prevent blood from flowing backwards, ensuring it moves in one direction only.
- Heartbeat: the rhythmic contraction (squeezing) and relaxation of the heart muscle that pumps blood around the body; each heartbeat can be felt as a pulse where an artery passes close to the skin, such as at the wrist or neck.

BLOOD VESSELS
- Arteries: thick-walled, muscular and elastic vessels that carry oxygenated blood away from the heart under high pressure to the rest of the body (the exception is the pulmonary artery, which carries deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs).
- Veins: thinner-walled vessels that carry deoxygenated blood back toward the heart under lower pressure; many veins contain valves to stop blood flowing backwards, especially in the limbs (the exception is the pulmonary vein, which carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart).
- Capillaries: extremely narrow, thin-walled vessels that connect the smallest arteries to the smallest veins; their thin walls allow oxygen, nutrients, carbon dioxide and other substances to pass between the blood and body tissues.

COMPOSITION AND FUNCTIONS OF BLOOD
- Red blood cells: carry oxygen around the body, giving blood its red colour.
- White blood cells: help defend the body against infection and disease.
- Platelets: help blood clot to seal cuts and wounds, preventing excessive blood loss.
- Plasma: the pale yellow liquid part of blood that carries blood cells, nutrients, hormones and waste products around the body.

THE DOUBLE CIRCULATION SYSTEM
Blood travels through the body in two connected loops:
1. Pulmonary circulation: deoxygenated blood is pumped from the right side of the heart to the lungs, where it picks up oxygen and releases carbon dioxide, before returning to the left side of the heart.
2. Systemic circulation: oxygenated blood is pumped from the left side of the heart to the rest of the body, delivering oxygen and nutrients to tissues, before returning as deoxygenated blood to the right side of the heart.

HOW EXERCISE AFFECTS THE CIRCULATORY SYSTEM
During exercise, working muscles need more oxygen and nutrients, and produce more carbon dioxide and other waste products. To meet this demand:
- Heart rate increases: the heart beats faster to pump blood around the body more quickly.
- Stroke volume increases: the heart also pumps more blood with each beat.
- Blood is redirected: more blood flow is sent to the working muscles and less to organs that are less active during exercise, such as the digestive system.
Regular physical activity over time makes the heart muscle stronger, allowing it to pump more blood with each beat (increased stroke volume) and often resulting in a lower resting heart rate, a common sign of good cardiovascular fitness.

KEEPING THE CIRCULATORY SYSTEM HEALTHY
- Regular physical activity strengthens the heart muscle.
- A balanced diet low in excess fat helps keep blood vessels clear and healthy.
- Avoiding harmful substances such as tobacco protects the heart and blood vessels.
- Adequate rest allows the heart and body to recover after exercise.

SUMMARY
- The heart is a muscular pump with four chambers (two atria, two ventricles) that circulates blood continuously.
- Arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins carry it back, and capillaries allow exchange of substances with body tissues.
- Blood is made of red blood cells, white blood cells, platelets and plasma, each with a specific function.
- Blood travels in two connected loops: pulmonary circulation (to and from the lungs) and systemic circulation (to and from the rest of the body).
- Exercise increases heart rate and stroke volume, and regular training strengthens the heart over time.

GLOSSARY
Atrium (plural atria): one of the two upper chambers of the heart that receive blood.
Ventricle: one of the two lower, more muscular chambers of the heart that pump blood out.
Stroke volume: the amount of blood pumped out of the heart with each single heartbeat.
Pulse: the rhythmic expansion of an artery felt at the wrist or neck, caused by each heartbeat.
source: Adapted from the ZIMSEC/Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education Junior (Grade 3-7) Physical Education, Sport and Mass Displays Syllabus (2015-2022), Topic 1

subject: Physical Education
topic: Safety and Health: Healthy Living Habits and the Activity Diary
content:
TOPIC 2, SUBTOPIC A: HEALTHY LIVING HABITS AND THE PHYSICAL ACTIVITY DIARY (Grade 7)

OBJECTIVES
Learners should be able to:
- describe healthy living habits at home, at school and in the community
- explain why each habit protects health
- keep and interpret a simple physical activity diary
- set personal goals for improving activity levels

WHAT IS HEALTHY LIVING?
Healthy living means making regular choices in daily life that protect and improve physical, mental and social wellbeing. For a Grade 7 learner, healthy living habits fall into three settings: home, school and community.

1. HEALTHY HABITS AT HOME
- Eating a balanced diet at each meal, including carbohydrates, proteins, vitamins, minerals and enough water.
- Washing hands with soap before eating and after using the toilet, to prevent the spread of germs.
- Bathing regularly to keep the skin clean and prevent skin infections.
- Brushing teeth at least twice a day to prevent tooth decay and gum disease.
- Getting enough sleep each night (Grade 7 learners generally need about 9-11 hours) so the body and mind can rest and recover.
- Drinking clean, safe water, boiled or treated if the source is not known to be safe.
- Keeping the home compound clean and free of standing water, which can breed mosquitoes.
- Doing household chores that involve movement (sweeping, fetching water, gardening), which count as valuable physical activity.

2. HEALTHY HABITS AT SCHOOL
- Washing hands before eating break-time food or lunch, and after using school toilets.
- Using clean toilets and reporting any that are blocked or dirty to a teacher.
- Drinking safe water provided at school, using a personal cup or bottle where possible.
- Wearing appropriate, comfortable clothing and footwear for Physical Education lessons.
- Participating actively and fully in Physical Education and sport, rather than sitting out unnecessarily.
- Respecting shared equipment and returning it after use so it stays in good, safe condition for others.

3. HEALTHY HABITS IN THE COMMUNITY
- Keeping the community environment clean by disposing of litter properly rather than throwing it on the ground.
- Avoiding or clearing stagnant water around the home and neighbourhood to prevent mosquitoes breeding (mosquitoes spread malaria).
- Taking part in community clean-up campaigns and group fitness or sporting activities.
- Respecting public health guidance, such as covering the mouth when coughing and staying home when seriously ill, to avoid spreading illness to others.

THE PHYSICAL ACTIVITY DIARY
A physical activity diary is a simple written or drawn record that a learner keeps, usually daily or weekly, of the physical activities they take part in. It should record:
- the type of activity (e.g. walking to school, playing football, skipping rope, dancing, doing chores that involve movement)
- roughly how long the activity lasted
- how the learner felt during and after the activity (e.g. tired, energetic, out of breath)

Why keep an activity diary?
- It helps a learner see clearly how active (or inactive) they really are across a week, rather than guessing.
- It helps identify days or periods with very little activity, so the learner can plan to be more active.
- It allows a learner to set simple, realistic personal goals, for example: 'I will walk or play actively for at least 30 minutes on 5 days this week.'
- Over weeks and months, it shows progress, which can be motivating.
- A teacher can use activity diaries to see which learners may need encouragement to be more physically active.

A SIMPLE WEEKLY ACTIVITY DIARY FORMAT
Day | Activity | Approx. duration | How I felt
Monday | Walked to school, played football at break | 40 minutes | Energetic
Tuesday | Helped sweep the yard, skipping rope | 25 minutes | A little tired
(and so on for each day of the week)

SETTING PERSONAL GOALS FROM THE DIARY
After reviewing a week's diary, a learner might notice, for example, that they were very active on some days but did almost nothing on others. A good personal goal responds directly to this pattern, such as choosing one specific inactive day and adding a short walk, some skipping, or a short game with friends on that day. Goals should be realistic, specific and reviewed regularly (for example, checked again after two weeks) to see if they were achieved.

SUMMARY
- Healthy living habits at home, school and in the community work together to prevent disease and support fitness.
- Hygiene (handwashing, bathing, clean toilets), nutrition, sleep, and an active lifestyle are all part of healthy living.
- A physical activity diary is a simple daily/weekly record used to track and improve how active a learner is.
- Reviewing the diary helps a learner set realistic, specific personal goals for becoming more active.

GLOSSARY
Hygiene: practices that keep the body and surroundings clean to prevent disease.
Activity diary: a written record of the physical activities a person takes part in over a period of time.
Personal goal: a specific target a learner sets for themselves, such as being active for a set amount of time each day.
source: Adapted from the ZIMSEC/Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education Junior (Grade 3-7) Physical Education, Sport and Mass Displays Syllabus (2015-2022), Topic 2

subject: Physical Education
topic: Safety and Health: Diseases from Poor Nutrition and Poor Sanitation
content:
TOPIC 2, SUBTOPIC B: DISEASES CAUSED BY POOR NUTRITION AND POOR SANITATION (Grade 7)

OBJECTIVES
Learners should be able to:
- identify diseases caused by lack of specific nutrients
- identify diseases caused by poor sanitary conditions and lack of exercise
- describe the signs/symptoms, causes and prevention of each disease
- explain the link between poor health and reduced ability to take part in physical activity

A. DISEASES CAUSED BY LACK OF EXERCISE
Regular physical activity keeps muscles, the heart and lungs strong. A lack of exercise over time can contribute to:
- Obesity: carrying excess body weight/fat, which places extra strain on the heart, joints and lungs, and can reduce a person's ability to take part comfortably in sport.
- Poor cardiovascular fitness: a heart and lungs that are not conditioned to cope well with physical effort, leading to becoming out of breath or tired very quickly during activity.
- Weak muscles and joints: reduced strength and flexibility, increasing the risk of injury during sudden physical effort.
Prevention: taking part in regular physical activity of at least moderate intensity most days of the week, combined with a balanced diet.

B. DISEASES CAUSED BY LACK OF SPECIFIC NUTRIENTS (MALNUTRITION)
1. Kwashiorkor
- Cause: severe lack of protein in the diet, even when overall energy (calorie) intake may be adequate.
- Signs: a swollen abdomen (stomach), thin arms and legs, swelling of the feet, changes in skin and hair colour (hair may turn reddish or lighter), general weakness and irritability.
- Prevention: eating protein-rich foods regularly, such as meat, fish, eggs, milk, beans, groundnuts and other legumes.
2. Marasmus
- Cause: severe overall lack of food, meaning both energy and protein intake are far too low over a long period.
- Signs: extreme thinness, visible ribs and bones, dry loose skin, weakness and stunted growth.
- Prevention: ensuring an adequate overall diet with enough calories from a variety of food groups.
3. Rickets
- Cause: lack of vitamin D and/or calcium, both needed for strong bone development.
- Signs: soft, weak or bent (bowed) bones, especially in the legs, delayed growth, and sometimes dental problems.
- Prevention: adequate sunlight exposure (which helps the body produce vitamin D), and eating calcium-rich foods such as milk, dairy products and small fish eaten with bones.
4. Anaemia
- Cause: lack of iron in the diet, reducing the blood's ability to carry oxygen effectively.
- Signs: constant tiredness, pale skin and inside of the eyelids, shortness of breath during activity, dizziness.
- Prevention: eating iron-rich foods such as leafy green vegetables, liver, meat and legumes.
5. Goitre
- Cause: lack of iodine in the diet, affecting the thyroid gland in the neck.
- Signs: visible swelling at the front of the neck (the thyroid gland enlarging).
- Prevention: using iodised salt and eating foods naturally containing iodine.

C. DISEASES CAUSED BY POOR SANITARY CONDITIONS
1. Cholera
- Cause: bacteria spread through water or food contaminated with faeces, often linked to unsafe water sources and poor sewage disposal.
- Signs: sudden, severe watery diarrhoea and vomiting, which can quickly lead to dangerous dehydration.
- Prevention: drinking only clean/boiled or treated water, washing hands with soap, safely disposing of human waste using proper toilets, and keeping food covered and clean.
2. Typhoid
- Cause: bacteria spread through food or water contaminated by an infected person's waste.
- Signs: prolonged fever, headache, stomach pain, and sometimes a rash.
- Prevention: safe water and food handling, good personal hygiene, and proper sanitation.
3. Diarrhoea and dysentery
- Cause: various germs from dirty water, unwashed hands, or poorly prepared or stored food.
- Signs: frequent loose or watery stools, stomach cramps, and in dysentery, sometimes blood in the stool.
- Prevention: safe water, thorough handwashing, properly cooked food, and clean food storage.

D. THE LINK BETWEEN HEALTH AND PHYSICAL ACTIVITY
Learners suffering from malnutrition or sanitation-related diseases often lack the energy, strength or stamina to participate fully in Physical Education and sport. Chronic poor nutrition can also stunt growth and weaken bones and muscles, directly affecting sporting performance. This is why Physical Education syllabuses place strong emphasis on nutrition and sanitation alongside physical skills - a learner cannot perform well physically without a healthy body to begin with.

SUMMARY
- Lack of exercise contributes to obesity, poor fitness and weak muscles/joints.
- Malnutrition diseases (kwashiorkor, marasmus, rickets, anaemia, goitre) each result from lacking a specific nutrient and have distinct signs.
- Sanitation-related diseases (cholera, typhoid, diarrhoea/dysentery) are spread through contaminated water or food and are prevented through hygiene and safe sanitation.
- Good nutrition and sanitation are essential foundations for full participation in physical activity and sport.

GLOSSARY
Malnutrition: poor health resulting from an inadequate or unbalanced diet.
Dehydration: a harmful lack of water in the body, often caused by severe diarrhoea or vomiting.
Sanitation: systems and practices, especially relating to water and waste disposal, that protect public health.
source: Adapted from the ZIMSEC/Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education Junior (Grade 3-7) Physical Education, Sport and Mass Displays Syllabus (2015-2022), Topic 2

subject: Physical Education
topic: Safety and Health: Safety Rules and First Aid
content:
TOPIC 2, SUBTOPIC C: SAFETY RULES AND FIRST AID DURING PHYSICAL ACTIVITY (Grade 7)

OBJECTIVES
Learners should be able to:
- apply safety rules before, during and after physical activity
- identify common causes of sporting injuries
- give appropriate basic first aid for common minor injuries
- explain when and how to get help for a serious injury

SAFETY RULES BEFORE PHYSICAL ACTIVITY
- Wear suitable clothing and footwear for the specific activity (e.g. proper sports shoes, not sandals, for running games).
- Remove jewellery, watches and any sharp objects that could cause injury to yourself or others.
- Check the playing area thoroughly for hazards such as stones, broken glass, holes, wet or slippery patches, before starting.
- Check that equipment (balls, bats, mats, goalposts) is in good condition and set up safely and securely.
- Always warm up properly with light jogging, dynamic stretches and activity-specific movements to prepare the muscles and joints.
- Drink water beforehand, especially in hot weather, to avoid starting an activity already dehydrated.

SAFETY RULES DURING PHYSICAL ACTIVITY
- Follow the rules of the activity or game at all times.
- Follow all instructions given by the teacher, coach or official.
- Avoid rough, reckless or dangerous play that could injure yourself or others (e.g. dangerous tackles, throwing equipment carelessly).
- Use equipment only for its intended purpose and in the way demonstrated by the teacher.
- Be aware of other learners around you to avoid collisions, especially during running or throwing activities.
- Drink water during breaks if the activity is long or the weather is hot, to prevent dehydration.
- Stop immediately and inform the teacher if you feel unwell, dizzy, or experience pain.

SAFETY RULES AFTER PHYSICAL ACTIVITY
- Always cool down with gentle movement and stretching to help the body recover gradually.
- Report any injury, no matter how minor it seems, to the teacher.
- Return equipment properly and store it safely so it does not become a hazard for others.
- Rehydrate and, where needed, eat to help the body recover.

COMMON CAUSES OF SPORTING INJURIES
- Skipping a proper warm-up, leaving muscles unprepared for sudden effort.
- Using damaged, unsafe, or incorrectly set up equipment.
- Playing on an unsafe or poorly checked surface.
- Ignoring rules or safety instructions, or engaging in reckless play.
- Overexertion - attempting an activity beyond one's current fitness or skill level without proper preparation.

FIRST AID: KEY PRINCIPLES
First aid is the immediate, temporary help given to an injured or suddenly ill person before proper medical treatment can be given. When giving first aid, a learner or teacher should:
1. Stay calm and reassure the injured person.
2. Check the situation is safe before approaching (e.g. no ongoing danger).
3. Give simple, appropriate first aid within one's knowledge and ability.
4. Get an adult or medical help quickly for anything beyond minor injuries.

FIRST AID FOR COMMON MINOR INJURIES
1. Cuts and grazes
- Clean the wound gently with clean water.
- Cover with a clean cloth, gauze or plaster to protect it from dirt and germs.
- Inform a teacher, especially if the cut is deep or bleeding heavily.
2. Sprains and strains (e.g. a twisted ankle)
- Stop the activity immediately; do not continue playing on the injury.
- Rest the injured part and avoid putting weight on it.
- Apply a cold compress (a clean cloth soaked in cool water, or an ice pack wrapped in cloth) if available, to reduce swelling.
- Elevate (raise) the injured limb if possible, and seek help from a teacher or adult.
3. Nosebleeds
- Sit the learner down and lean the head slightly forward (not backward, to avoid blood running down the throat).
- Gently pinch the soft part of the nose for several minutes.
- Seek adult help if bleeding does not stop after a reasonable time.
4. Fainting
- Help the learner lie down safely, or sit with the head lowered between the knees if lying down is not possible.
- Loosen any tight clothing around the neck.
- Ensure fresh air and space around the learner.
- Call a teacher or adult immediately.
5. Insect bites/stings
- Remove any visible sting carefully without squeezing it.
- Clean the area with water.
- Watch for signs of a serious allergic reaction (difficulty breathing, severe swelling) and get emergency medical help immediately if these occur.

WHEN TO SEEK URGENT MEDICAL HELP
A teacher or responsible adult should be called immediately, and emergency medical help sought, for injuries such as: suspected broken bones, deep or heavily bleeding wounds, loss of consciousness, difficulty breathing, a serious head injury, or any injury the first-aider is unsure how to handle safely.

SUMMARY
- Safety rules apply before (preparation, checking area/equipment), during (following rules, awareness) and after (cooling down, reporting injuries) physical activity.
- Most sporting injuries are caused by poor preparation, unsafe equipment/surfaces, or reckless play.
- Basic first aid can be given for common minor injuries such as cuts, sprains, nosebleeds, fainting and insect bites.
- Serious injuries always require immediate adult help and, where necessary, emergency medical attention.

GLOSSARY
First aid: immediate, temporary care given to an injured or suddenly ill person before professional medical help arrives.
Sprain: an injury to a ligament (tissue connecting bones at a joint) caused by twisting or overstretching.
Cold compress: a cold, damp cloth or ice pack applied to an injury to reduce swelling and pain.
source: Adapted from the ZIMSEC/Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education Junior (Grade 3-7) Physical Education, Sport and Mass Displays Syllabus (2015-2022), Topic 2

subject: Physical Education
topic: Aquatic Skills: Water Safety and Personnel
content:
TOPIC 3, SUBTOPIC A: WATER SAFETY RULES AND AQUATIC PERSONNEL (Grade 7)

OBJECTIVES
Learners should be able to:
- state and explain water safety rules
- describe the roles of different aquatic personnel
- identify common water safety equipment
- explain the dangers associated with unsafe water behaviour

WHY WATER SAFETY COMES FIRST
Water can be extremely dangerous even for confident swimmers, especially when rules are ignored. Before any swimming or aquatic skill is taught, learners must understand and commit to following clear water safety rules, since drowning can happen very quickly and silently.

KEY WATER SAFETY RULES
1. Never swim alone. Always swim with a partner ('the buddy system') or under the direct supervision of an adult or lifeguard.
2. Always obey the lifeguard's instructions immediately, without arguing or delaying.
3. Never run, push or engage in rough play in or around the pool, as this can cause slipping, collisions or accidental drowning.
4. Never dive into water of unknown or shallow depth - always check depth markers or ask a lifeguard first.
5. Do not spit, urinate or throw litter into swimming water, both for hygiene and to keep the water safe and pleasant for everyone.
6. Avoid swimming immediately after eating a heavy meal, as this can cause cramps or discomfort.
7. Know your own swimming ability and never attempt to swim beyond it, such as venturing into deep water when unable to swim confidently.
8. Enter unfamiliar water feet-first rather than diving, until the depth and any underwater hazards are known.
9. Learn the location of safety equipment such as ropes, rescue rings, poles and floating aids before entering the water.
10. Pay attention to warning signs and flags at rivers, dams or pools, which may indicate danger such as strong currents or restricted swimming areas.
11. Never swim during a thunderstorm, as water conducts electricity and increases the danger from lightning.
12. Be extra cautious in natural water bodies (rivers, dams), which may have hidden currents, drop-offs, or underwater debris not present in a controlled pool environment.

COMMON WATER SAFETY EQUIPMENT
- Rescue ring (life ring): a circular floating ring thrown to a struggling swimmer to help them stay afloat.
- Rescue pole/reaching pole: a long pole used by a rescuer to reach a struggling swimmer without entering the water themselves.
- Rope: used to throw to a swimmer in difficulty, or as a barrier marking safe swimming zones.
- Floating aids (e.g. kickboards, pool noodles): used both for teaching swimming and for emergency floatation support.
- Whistle: used by lifeguards to gain attention quickly, such as to warn of danger or stop dangerous behaviour.

ROLES OF AQUATIC PERSONNEL
1. Lifeguard
- Constantly watches all swimmers in their area, scanning for signs of difficulty such as unusual splashing, a swimmer going quiet, or a swimmer's head low in the water.
- Enforces pool/water safety rules and stops dangerous behaviour immediately.
- Performs rescues when a swimmer is in difficulty, using appropriate techniques and equipment.
- Administers first aid, including resuscitation if trained and necessary, until further medical help arrives.
2. Swimming coach
- Teaches correct swimming technique for different strokes.
- Plans training sessions to build stamina, speed and skill in swimmers.
- Prepares competitive swimmers for galas and competitions.
3. Starter
- Officiates at swimming competitions by giving the official starting signal (often a whistle, horn or starting gun) for a race to begin.
- Watches for false starts, where a swimmer begins before the signal.
4. Timekeeper
- Records the exact time each swimmer takes to complete their race, used to determine placing and results.
- Works with other timekeepers/officials to confirm accurate results.

WHY THESE RULES AND ROLES MATTER
Understanding water safety rules and the roles of aquatic personnel helps learners behave responsibly around water, know who to listen to and trust in an aquatic setting, and understand that aquatic activities, while enjoyable, require serious respect for safety at all times.

SUMMARY
- Water safety rules must always be followed before any swimming activity is attempted.
- Never swim alone, never dive into unknown depths, and always obey the lifeguard.
- Rescue rings, poles, ropes and floating aids are common water safety equipment.
- Lifeguards, coaches, starters and timekeepers each play a distinct, important role in keeping aquatic activities safe and well organised.

GLOSSARY
Buddy system: a safety practice of always swimming with a partner rather than alone.
Lifeguard: a trained person who supervises swimmers and performs rescues when needed.
Rescue ring: a floating ring thrown to a swimmer in difficulty to help them stay afloat.
source: Adapted from the ZIMSEC/Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education Junior (Grade 3-7) Physical Education, Sport and Mass Displays Syllabus (2015-2022), Topic 3

subject: Physical Education
topic: Aquatic Skills: Swimming Strokes and Technique
content:
TOPIC 3, SUBTOPIC B: SWIMMING STROKES AND TECHNIQUE (Grade 7)

OBJECTIVES
Learners should be able to:
- describe the technique of each of the four main swimming strokes
- explain the correct breathing pattern for each stroke
- identify common technique errors and how to correct them
- explain which stroke is generally taught first to beginners and why

OVERVIEW OF THE FOUR MAIN STROKES
Swimming strokes are the different techniques used to move through water efficiently. The four internationally recognised competitive strokes are front crawl (freestyle), backstroke, breaststroke and butterfly. At Grade 7 level, learners focus on understanding and practising the basic technique of each.

1. FRONT CRAWL (FREESTYLE)
- Body position: the swimmer lies face-down and as flat as possible near the water's surface, with the body streamlined from head to toe.
- Arm action: alternating overarm strokes - one arm pulls through the water while the other recovers above the water, in a continuous, rotating motion.
- Leg action: a continuous flutter kick, with legs alternating up and down from the hips, feet relaxed and toes pointed.
- Breathing: the swimmer turns the head to one side to breathe in during the arm recovery, then turns the face back down into the water to breathe out.
- Notes: generally considered the fastest of the four common strokes, widely used in freestyle and triathlon events.
Common errors: lifting the head too high to breathe (which drops the legs and slows the swimmer down), and kicking from the knees instead of the hips (reducing propulsion).

2. BACKSTROKE
- Body position: the swimmer lies face-up on the back, body as flat and streamlined as possible.
- Arm action: alternating overarm strokes, similar in rhythm to front crawl but performed on the back, with arms recovering over the water and pulling underwater on the opposite side.
- Leg action: a continuous flutter kick, similar to front crawl but performed while facing upward.
- Breathing: since the face remains above the water, breathing can be done freely and does not need to be timed with arm movement, making this a good stroke for beginners to practise breathing control.
- Notes: because the swimmer faces upward, care must be taken to swim in a straight line, often using overhead lane markers, flags or backstroke flags found in pools as a guide.
Common errors: sitting too low in the water (hips dropping), and an uneven or inconsistent kick.

3. BREASTSTROKE
- Body position: the swimmer lies face-down, body relatively flat, with the head lifting for breathing at a specific point in the stroke cycle.
- Arm action: both arms move together and symmetrically - pulling outward and backward in a semi-circular pattern, then recovering forward close to the chest and body, before extending forward again.
- Leg action: a 'whip kick' or 'frog kick' - both legs move together, bending at the knees and hips, then whipping outward and backward before snapping together, propelling the swimmer forward.
- Breathing: the swimmer lifts the head and shoulders to breathe in as the arms pull and the body rises slightly, then lowers the face back into the water during the glide and kick.
- Notes: often the first full stroke taught to beginners because the head can remain above water for longer periods, making it feel safer and more controlled; it is a slower stroke than front crawl but requires good coordination between arms, legs and breathing.
Common errors: kicking with a scissor action instead of a symmetrical whip kick, and poor timing between the arm pull and leg kick.

4. BUTTERFLY
- Body position: face-down, with an undulating (wave-like) body motion from head to toe.
- Arm action: both arms move together, pulling backward through the water simultaneously in a semi-circular pattern, then recovering forward together over the water's surface.
- Leg action: a 'dolphin kick' - both legs move together in an up-and-down wave-like motion, similar to a dolphin's tail, often performed in a rhythm of two kicks per arm cycle.
- Breathing: the head lifts forward to breathe as the arms complete their pull and begin recovery, then lowers back into the water during the arm recovery and kick.
- Notes: considered the most physically demanding of the four strokes, requiring strong core, shoulder and leg strength, and good timing between the arm pull, body undulation and kick; usually introduced only once a learner is confident and competent in the other three strokes.
Common errors: lifting the head too high or too late (disrupting the wave rhythm), and a weak or poorly timed dolphin kick.

ORDER OF TEACHING STROKES
At primary school level, learners typically build basic water confidence first (see the next subtopic), then are introduced to breaststroke and/or front crawl before progressing to backstroke, with butterfly usually introduced last due to its higher physical demands and technical difficulty.

GENERAL TECHNIQUE PRINCIPLES ACROSS ALL STROKES
- Streamlining: keeping the body as flat, straight and narrow as possible in the water reduces resistance (drag) and improves speed and efficiency.
- Rhythm and timing: coordinating arm movement, leg movement and breathing smoothly, rather than performing each part separately or in a rushed, jerky manner.
- Relaxation: unnecessary tension in the body (e.g. a tense neck or clenched fists) wastes energy and can reduce a swimmer's efficiency.

SUMMARY
- The four main swimming strokes are front crawl, backstroke, breaststroke and butterfly, each with a distinct body position, arm action, leg action and breathing pattern.
- Breaststroke is often taught first to beginners because breathing feels more controlled; butterfly is usually taught last due to its physical demands.
- Good technique across all strokes depends on streamlining, rhythm/timing and relaxation.
- Learners should be aware of common technique errors so they can self-correct or seek help from an instructor.

GLOSSARY
Streamlining: shaping the body to move through water with minimal resistance.
Flutter kick: an alternating up-and-down leg kick used in front crawl and backstroke.
Whip kick (frog kick): the simultaneous, circular leg action used in breaststroke.
Dolphin kick: the simultaneous up-and-down wave-like leg action used in butterfly.
source: Adapted from the ZIMSEC/Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education Junior (Grade 3-7) Physical Education, Sport and Mass Displays Syllabus (2015-2022), Topic 3

subject: Physical Education
topic: Aquatic Skills: Water Confidence and Emergency Response
content:
TOPIC 3, SUBTOPIC C: WATER CONFIDENCE SKILLS AND EMERGENCY RESPONSE (Grade 7)

OBJECTIVES
Learners should be able to:
- perform basic water confidence skills
- explain the purpose of each confidence-building skill
- describe what to do if someone is in danger in water
- explain the correct order of actions in a water emergency

WATER CONFIDENCE SKILLS
Before learning full swimming strokes, learners build water confidence through foundational skills that help them feel comfortable, safe and in control in water.
1. Getting used to water on the face: splashing water gently on the face, then progressing to blowing bubbles with the mouth and nose just below the surface, helping a learner become comfortable with water around the face.
2. Submerging: gently lowering the whole head underwater for a few seconds, opening the eyes underwater if goggles are available, building comfort with being fully submerged.
3. Floating on the front: lying face-down on the water's surface with arms and legs relaxed and spread, using a held breath or light kicking to stay near the surface; this teaches a learner that the body is naturally buoyant.
4. Floating on the back: lying face-up on the water's surface with the head tilted back slightly (ears in the water) and arms/legs relaxed, allowing calm, controlled breathing while floating.
5. Treading water: staying upright in deep water without touching the bottom, using small circular or scissor-like movements of the arms and legs to stay afloat in one place; a vital survival skill.
6. Basic kicking drills: practising the flutter kick while holding the pool edge, a kickboard, or with support from an instructor, to build leg strength and coordination before combining it with arm strokes.
7. Gliding: pushing off gently from the pool wall or floor in a streamlined position and gliding through the water without kicking, to feel how the body moves efficiently through water.

WHY THESE SKILLS MATTER
Each confidence skill builds toward safe, independent swimming: floating and treading water are essential survival skills even for a non-swimmer who accidentally enters deep water, while submerging and getting used to water on the face remove fear and hesitation that can make full strokes difficult to learn.

RECOGNISING A WATER EMERGENCY
Signs that a swimmer may be in trouble include:
- Head low in the water, with mouth at water level.
- Arms pressing down on the water's surface rather than being used to swim.
- The swimmer appearing to climb an invisible ladder.
- Very little or no kicking.
- The swimmer being unusually quiet, unable to call out or wave for help (real drowning is often silent, unlike dramatic depictions in films).

WHAT TO DO IN A WATER EMERGENCY (CORRECT ORDER OF ACTIONS)
1. Shout for help immediately, alerting the lifeguard, a teacher or the nearest responsible adult; do not waste time trying to handle a serious situation entirely alone.
2. Do not jump into the water to attempt a rescue unless you are trained in water rescue, since an untrained rescuer can easily be pulled under by a panicking swimmer, creating two victims instead of one.
3. Reach for the person if they are close enough, using a pole, rope, branch, item of clothing or any long object, while keeping your own feet firmly on solid ground or a stable surface.
4. Throw a floating object (rescue ring, empty plastic container, kickboard, or anything that floats) to the person so they have something to hold on to and stay afloat.
5. Row or use a boat only if trained and one is safely available, to reach a person too far away to reach or throw to.
6. Only go (swim out) as an absolute last resort, and only if trained in rescue technique, since this carries the greatest risk to the rescuer.
This order is sometimes remembered as: Reach, Throw, Row, Go - starting with the safest option for the rescuer and only moving to riskier options for the rescuer if nothing else is possible.

AFTER A RESCUE
- If the person is unconscious or not breathing normally once out of the water, call for emergency medical help immediately.
- If trained in first aid/resuscitation, begin appropriate first aid while waiting for help to arrive.
- Keep the rescued person calm, warm and lying down until medical help arrives.
- Never assume a person is 'fine' simply because they are conscious after a near-drowning incident; medical checks are still important, as water can sometimes enter the lungs without immediately obvious symptoms.

SUMMARY
- Water confidence skills (getting used to water on the face, submerging, floating, treading water, kicking drills, gliding) build the foundation for safe swimming.
- Recognising the quiet, often undramatic signs of a swimmer in real difficulty is an important safety skill.
- In an emergency, the safest order of action for an untrained rescuer is: shout for help, reach, then throw a floating object - never swim out unless trained.
- After any rescue, medical help should be sought, and the person should never be left alone or assumed to be completely fine.

GLOSSARY
Treading water: staying upright and afloat in deep water without touching the bottom, using continuous small movements of the arms and legs.
Submerging: lowering the body, including the head, fully under the water's surface.
Reach, Throw, Row, Go: the safety order of rescue actions, starting with the option safest for the rescuer.
source: Adapted from the ZIMSEC/Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education Junior (Grade 3-7) Physical Education, Sport and Mass Displays Syllabus (2015-2022), Topic 3

subject: Physical Education
topic: Kids Athletics: Running and Track Events
content:
TOPIC 4, SUBTOPIC A: RUNNING AND TRACK EVENTS (Grade 7)

OBJECTIVES
Learners should be able to:
- perform correct sprinting technique
- distinguish between sprint, middle-distance and relay events
- describe the phases of a sprint race
- explain the rules and common infringements of track events

TYPES OF RUNNING (TRACK) EVENTS
1. Sprints: short, high-speed races such as 50m, 60m, 80m and 100m, testing pure speed and acceleration over a short distance.
2. Middle-distance races: longer races such as 400m, 600m or 800m, requiring a balance of speed and endurance, and good pacing (not sprinting flat-out for the entire distance).
3. Relay races: team events in which a team of usually four runners each complete a section (leg) of the total distance, passing a baton to the next runner within a marked changeover (takeover) zone.
4. Obstacle/hurdle-style events (adapted for kids athletics): running events that include safe, low obstacles to jump or step over, developing rhythm, coordination and confidence around obstacles without full hurdling technique.

PHASES OF A SPRINT RACE
1. The start: the athlete takes a set position (standing or crouched, depending on age/level) behind the start line, waiting for the starting signal without moving early.
2. Acceleration (drive phase): immediately after the start, the athlete drives forward with powerful, low, driving steps, gradually rising to an upright running posture over the first several metres.
3. Maximum speed phase: the athlete reaches top running speed, maintaining a tall, relaxed posture with a strong arm drive and high knee lift.
4. Speed maintenance/finish: as fatigue sets in near the end of the race, the athlete focuses on maintaining good technique and running speed through the finish line, rather than slowing down before crossing it.

CORRECT SPRINTING TECHNIQUE
- Head: kept steady and looking forward, not looking down or side to side.
- Arms: driven strongly forward and backward from the shoulder, bent at roughly a right angle at the elbow, hands relaxed (not clenched into tight fists).
- Trunk: leaning very slightly forward, especially during acceleration, becoming more upright at maximum speed.
- Legs: driving powerfully from the hips, with a high knee lift and a strong push-off from the toes/balls of the feet.
- Foot strike: landing on the balls of the feet rather than flat-footed or on the heels, allowing a quick, springy contact with the ground.

RELAY RACES
- The baton: a short tube passed from one runner to the next; it must be carried by hand throughout the race and passed within the designated changeover zone.
- The changeover (takeover) zone: a marked section of the track within which the outgoing runner must receive the baton from the incoming runner; passing outside this zone results in disqualification of the team.
- Techniques for passing: the outgoing runner usually begins moving before the incoming runner arrives, reaching back (without looking, in more advanced technique, or looking back for younger/beginner learners) to receive the baton smoothly without slowing down excessively.
- Team communication: often a verbal cue (such as calling 'stick' or 'hand') is used by the incoming runner to signal the outgoing runner to reach back for the baton.

COMMON RULES AND INFRINGEMENTS IN TRACK EVENTS
- Lane discipline: in sprint races, athletes must stay within their own marked lane from start to finish; leaving your lane and interfering with another athlete can lead to disqualification.
- False start: starting to move before the official starting signal is given; depending on the level of competition, this can result in a warning or disqualification, especially on a repeated false start.
- Baton passing rules: the baton must be exchanged within the marked changeover zone; dropping the baton means the same team member who dropped it (or the one due to receive it) must retrieve it, and the team continues, though valuable time is lost.
- Obstruction: deliberately blocking or interfering with another runner is not allowed and can result in disqualification.

OFFICIALS INVOLVED IN TRACK EVENTS
- Starter: gives the official signal to begin the race and watches for false starts.
- Timekeepers: record the time taken by each athlete to complete the race.
- Track judges: watch for rule infringements such as lane violations or obstruction.
- Photo finish/finish line judges: determine the exact finishing order, especially in close races.

SUMMARY
- Track events include sprints (speed), middle-distance races (speed and endurance), relays (team baton-passing) and adapted obstacle-style events.
- A sprint race has clear phases: the start, acceleration, maximum speed and the finish.
- Correct technique involves a steady head, strong arm drive, forward lean during acceleration, high knee lift and landing on the balls of the feet.
- Relay races require the baton to be exchanged within a marked changeover zone using good technique and communication.
- Common infringements include lane violations, false starts and baton-passing errors outside the zone.

GLOSSARY
Acceleration phase: the early part of a sprint race where an athlete builds up from a stationary start to top speed.
Changeover (takeover) zone: the marked section of track within which a relay baton must be passed between runners.
False start: beginning a race before the official starting signal.
source: Adapted from the ZIMSEC/Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education Junior (Grade 3-7) Physical Education, Sport and Mass Displays Syllabus (2015-2022), Topic 4

subject: Physical Education
content:
TOPIC 4, SUBTOPIC B: JUMPING EVENTS (Grade 7)

OBJECTIVES
Learners should be able to:
- perform the basic technique of long jump and high jump
- describe the phases of a jump
- explain the rules and common fouls in jumping events
- explain the safety considerations for jumping events

LONG JUMP
The long jump tests an athlete's ability to jump for maximum horizontal distance from a running start.
Phases of the long jump:
1. The approach run: a controlled, accelerating run down a runway toward the take-off board, gradually building to near-maximum controlled speed.
2. Take-off: the athlete plants one foot firmly on or just behind the take-off board and drives upward and forward, converting horizontal running speed into a controlled jump.
3. Flight (action in the air): the athlete uses arm and leg movements (such as a 'hang' style, where the legs trail behind, or a hitch-kick/running style in the air) to maintain balance and prepare for landing.
4. Landing: the athlete extends both legs forward together, aiming to land as far forward as possible in the sandpit without falling backward, since the distance is measured from the take-off board to the nearest mark made in the sand.
Key technique points: an accurate, consistent approach run so take-off happens right at the board, a strong single-footed take-off, and a controlled landing with knees bent to absorb impact and legs extended fully forward.

HIGH JUMP
The high jump tests an athlete's ability to jump over a raised horizontal bar without knocking it down, landing safely on a cushioned mat.
Phases of the high jump:
1. The approach run: typically a curved run-up (in styles such as the Fosbury Flop used in senior athletics) or a straight approach for simpler styles used at primary level.
2. Take-off: a powerful push from one foot, converting forward speed into upward lift, timed to happen at an optimal distance and angle from the bar.
3. Flight/bar clearance: the athlete's body rotates and arches (or uses a scissor action in a simpler beginner style) to clear the bar without dislodging it.
4. Landing: the athlete lands safely on a soft, cushioned landing mat, usually on the back or shoulders for advanced styles, or on the feet for simpler beginner styles.
Simple styles suitable for Grade 7: the scissor jump/straddle-style approaches, which are safer and simpler to learn than advanced techniques like the Fosbury Flop, which requires specialised coaching and proper mat safety.

STANDING JUMPS
Standing jumps (for distance or height) are performed from a stationary position without a running approach, and are often used to build basic jumping strength, technique and confidence, especially for younger or beginner learners. Key technique: a deep bend of the knees and hips to load the legs, a strong simultaneous push from both feet, and full extension of the body in the air before landing with bent knees.

GENERAL JUMPING TECHNIQUE PRINCIPLES
- A consistent, controlled approach run improves accuracy at take-off.
- A strong, well-timed take-off converts running or standing power into upward and/or forward movement.
- Body control in the air helps maintain balance and prepare for a safe, effective landing.
- Landing with bent knees (never stiff, locked legs) absorbs impact and protects the joints from injury.

RULES AND COMMON FOULS IN JUMPING EVENTS
- Long jump: stepping on or beyond the take-off board/line during take-off results in a foul jump that does not count, even if the resulting distance would otherwise have been a personal best.
- Long jump: the measured distance is always taken from the closest mark made in the sandpit back to the take-off board/line, so falling or touching backward reduces the recorded distance.
- High jump: knocking the bar off its supports during the jump attempt (even if the athlete's body clears it) results in a failed attempt.
- High jump: athletes are usually allowed a set number of attempts (commonly three) at each height before being eliminated if unsuccessful.
- In both events, athletes must take off from one foot only (unless the specific event rules state otherwise for younger age groups).

SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
- Long jump: the sandpit must be raked level and free of stones, glass or debris before use; athletes should not walk back to the start line through the sandpit landing area.
- High jump: the landing mat must be thick, properly positioned directly behind the bar, and checked for stability before each attempt; the bar itself should be lightweight so it does not injure an athlete if dislodged.
- All jumping events: a clear queuing system and waiting for the previous athlete to finish and clear the area before the next attempt begins.

SUMMARY
- Long jump tests horizontal distance from a running take-off; high jump tests vertical height over a raised bar.
- Each jump has clear phases: approach, take-off, flight and landing.
- Standing jumps build foundational jumping strength and are useful for younger or beginner learners.
- Common fouls include stepping over the take-off line (long jump) and knocking the bar (high jump).
- Safety depends on well-prepared landing areas (raked sand, properly placed mats) and orderly queuing between attempts.

GLOSSARY
Take-off board: the marked line or board in long jump beyond which an athlete's foot must not cross at take-off.
Foul jump: a jump that does not count due to a rule violation, such as crossing the take-off line.
Scissor jump: a simple, beginner-level high jump technique where the legs move over the bar one after the other in a scissoring action.
source: Adapted from the ZIMSEC/Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education Junior (Grade 3-7) Physical Education, Sport and Mass Displays Syllabus (2015-2022), Topic 4

subject: Physical Education
content:
TOPIC 4, SUBTOPIC C: THROWING EVENTS (Grade 7)

OBJECTIVES
Learners should be able to:
- perform the basic technique of adapted throwing events
- describe the rules and safety procedures for throwing events
- distinguish between throws for distance and throws for accuracy
- explain the officiating roles involved in throwing events

TYPES OF THROWING EVENTS IN KIDS ATHLETICS
Kids Athletics uses safe, lightweight, adapted versions of the senior throwing events, allowing learners to develop throwing technique without the risks associated with full-weight adult implements.
1. Discus-style throw (adapted): using a light, soft discus-shaped implement, thrown either from a standing position or with a simple turning action, aiming for maximum distance within a marked sector.
2. Javelin-style throw (adapted): using a light, safe, javelin-style implement (often with a soft or blunt tip), thrown overarm from a short run-up or standing position for maximum distance.
3. Shot put-style push (adapted): using a lightweight ball or bag, 'pushed' rather than thrown from the shoulder and neck area, aiming for maximum distance; this is not a full throwing action, to protect the elbow and shoulder joints of young athletes.
4. Target/accuracy throws: throwing a ball or bean bag at a marked target or zone, scored by accuracy rather than distance.

BASIC TECHNIQUE PRINCIPLES
- Grip: holding the implement securely and comfortably, following the specific grip taught for that implement.
- Stance: standing side-on or facing the throwing direction, depending on the event, with feet positioned to allow a strong, balanced throwing action.
- Transfer of weight: shifting body weight from the back foot to the front foot as the throw is made, adding power to the throw.
- Release: releasing the implement at the correct angle and moment for maximum distance or accuracy, following through with the throwing arm afterward.
- Follow-through: continuing the throwing motion smoothly after release, rather than stopping abruptly, which helps maintain balance and technique.

SAFETY: THE MOST IMPORTANT PART OF THROWING EVENTS
Because throwing implements travel through the air and can injure someone if mishandled, safety procedures must be strictly followed:
- Throwers must never throw until an official gives a clear signal that the throwing area ahead is clear of people.
- No one is allowed to walk into the throwing sector/landing area until all implements have landed and been checked/retrieved.
- Throwers must always throw in the officially marked direction only, never towards spectators, other events, or areas where people may be present.
- Implements should be carried, not thrown, back to the throwing area after retrieval.
- Spectators and non-participating learners must stay well clear of the throwing area at all times.
- Any damaged or unsafe implement must be reported and not used.

RULES FOR DISTANCE THROWS (DISCUS-STYLE, JAVELIN-STYLE, SHOT-STYLE)
- The implement must land within the marked throwing sector (a wedge-shaped marked area) to count as a valid, measurable throw; a throw landing outside the sector lines does not count.
- The thrower must not step over the marked throwing line/circle before, during or immediately after the release, or the throw is disqualified as a foul.
- Distance is measured from the point where the implement first touches the ground back to the inside edge of the throwing circle/line.
- Athletes are usually given a set number of attempts (commonly three to six depending on the competition), with only the best valid distance counting toward their final result.

RULES FOR ACCURACY/TARGET THROWS
- Scoring is based on where the object lands relative to marked target zones (for example, a bullseye zone scoring the most points, with surrounding zones scoring progressively less).
- A clear queuing and turn-taking system must be followed, with only one thrower active at a time.

OFFICIALS INVOLVED IN THROWING EVENTS
- Judges: confirm whether a throw is valid (landed within the sector, no foul at the line) and measure the distance or determine the accuracy score.
- Safety marshals/officials: control access to the throwing and landing areas, ensuring no one enters until it is safe.
- Recorders: note down each athlete's results across their attempts.

SUMMARY
- Kids Athletics uses safe, adapted, lightweight versions of discus, javelin and shot put, alongside accuracy-based target throws.
- Good technique involves correct grip, stance, weight transfer, release and follow-through.
- Safety is the top priority: throwers must wait for a clear signal, throw only in the marked direction, and never enter the landing area until it is confirmed safe.
- Distance throws are judged by whether the implement lands within a marked sector and measured back to the throwing line; accuracy throws are scored by target zones.

GLOSSARY
Sector: the marked, wedge-shaped area within which a thrown implement must land to count as valid.
Follow-through: the continuation of a throwing (or striking) action smoothly after the object is released or hit.
Foul throw: a throw that does not count because a rule, such as stepping over the throwing line, was broken.
source: Adapted from the ZIMSEC/Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education Junior (Grade 3-7) Physical Education, Sport and Mass Displays Syllabus (2015-2022), Topic 4

subject: Physical Education
topic: Kids Athletics: Warming Up, Cooling Down and Officiating
content:
TOPIC 4, SUBTOPIC D: WARMING UP, COOLING DOWN AND OFFICIATING IN ATHLETICS (Grade 7)

OBJECTIVES
Learners should be able to:
- explain the purpose and structure of a proper warm-up
- explain the purpose and structure of a proper cool-down
- describe the general rules that apply across athletics events
- identify the officials involved in running an athletics competition

WHY WARMING UP MATTERS
A warm-up gradually prepares the body for the physical demands of athletics by raising muscle temperature, increasing heart rate and breathing rate gradually, and improving the flexibility and readiness of joints and muscles. A good warm-up significantly reduces the risk of injuries such as muscle strains, which are more likely when cold, stiff muscles are suddenly asked to perform explosive movements like sprinting, jumping or throwing.

STRUCTURE OF A GOOD ATHLETICS WARM-UP
1. General warm-up: light continuous activity such as jogging for several minutes to gradually raise heart rate, breathing rate and body temperature.
2. Mobility and dynamic stretching: controlled, moving stretches (such as leg swings, arm circles, walking lunges) that take joints through their full range of motion while the body stays moving, rather than static stretches held still for a long time (which are better saved for the cool-down).
3. Activity-specific preparation: movements that closely resemble the actual event to follow, such as short build-up sprints before a race, practice run-ups before jumping events, or light practice throws (with a safe, controlled implement) before throwing events.

WHY COOLING DOWN MATTERS
A cool-down allows the body to recover gradually from intense exercise rather than stopping abruptly. It helps the heart rate and breathing rate return to resting levels gradually, helps remove waste products that build up in muscles during hard exercise, and can reduce muscle stiffness and soreness in the following days.

STRUCTURE OF A GOOD COOL-DOWN
1. Light continuous activity: gentle jogging or walking for several minutes immediately after the event or session, allowing heart rate to come down gradually rather than suddenly stopping.
2. Static stretching: holding stretches for each major muscle group used during the session (e.g. hamstrings, quadriceps, calves, shoulders) for around 15-30 seconds each, which can help maintain flexibility over time.
3. Rehydration and rest: drinking water and allowing the body time to recover before further strenuous activity.

GENERAL RULES ACROSS ATHLETICS EVENTS
- All athletes must follow the specific rules of their event (lane discipline in track events, take-off/throwing line rules in field events).
- Athletes must respect officials' decisions and not argue disruptively with rulings.
- Athletes must wear appropriate athletics kit and footwear as required by the competition.
- Unsporting behaviour, such as deliberately obstructing another competitor, is not allowed and can lead to disqualification.
- Athletes should only compete in events for which they are properly registered/entered.

OFFICIALS INVOLVED IN AN ATHLETICS COMPETITION
- Meeting referee/chief official: has overall responsibility for ensuring the competition runs fairly and according to the rules, and makes final decisions on disputes.
- Starter: gives the official signal to begin track races and manages false starts.
- Track judges: monitor for rule violations during races, such as lane infringements.
- Timekeepers: record the time taken by athletes in track events.
- Field event judges: oversee jumping and throwing events, checking for fouls, measuring distances/heights, and recording results.
- Recorders: collect and record all results across events for the final competition results.

WHY OFFICIALS MATTER
Officials ensure that athletics competitions are conducted fairly, safely and according to agreed rules, giving every athlete an equal and fair chance to compete. Learners should understand and respect the role of officials, since a competition without clear rules and fair officiating would not be a meaningful contest of athletic ability.

SUMMARY
- A proper warm-up (general activity, dynamic stretching, activity-specific preparation) reduces injury risk and prepares the body for athletics events.
- A proper cool-down (light activity, static stretching, rehydration) helps the body recover after exertion.
- General athletics rules require following event-specific regulations, respecting officials, and avoiding unsporting behaviour.
- Officials such as the starter, judges, timekeepers and recorders each play a specific role in running a fair athletics competition.

GLOSSARY
Dynamic stretching: moving stretches performed as part of a warm-up, taking joints through their range of motion while the body stays active.
Static stretching: holding a single stretch position still, usually for 15-30 seconds, typically done during a cool-down.
Field events: athletics events involving jumping or throwing, as opposed to track (running) events.
source: Adapted from the ZIMSEC/Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education Junior (Grade 3-7) Physical Education, Sport and Mass Displays Syllabus (2015-2022), Topic 4

subject: Physical Education
content:
TOPIC 5, SUBTOPIC A: FOOTBALL (SOCCER) (Grade 7)

OBJECTIVES
Learners should be able to:
- demonstrate basic football skills
- explain the basic rules and common infringements of football
- identify player positions and their roles
- apply basic attacking and defending principles in football

BASIC SKILLS
1. Dribbling: moving the ball forward using a series of controlled touches with the feet, keeping the ball close so an opponent cannot easily win it; good dribbling uses both the inside and outside of the foot and includes changes of pace and direction to beat opponents.
2. Passing: sending the ball accurately to a teammate.
- Push pass (inside-of-foot pass): the most accurate short pass, using the inside of the foot to strike the ball firmly and directly.
- Instep/laces pass: used for longer, more powerful passes, striking the ball with the top of the foot (laces area).
- Outside-of-foot pass: used for quick, disguised passes in tight spaces.
3. Receiving/trapping: bringing an incoming ball under control using the foot (cushioning it on contact), thigh, chest, or occasionally the head, so the ball does not bounce away uncontrolled.
4. Shooting: striking the ball with power and/or accuracy toward the goal, often using the instep for power or the inside of the foot for placement/accuracy.
5. Heading: using the forehead (never the top of the head) to direct the ball, used for both attacking (heading toward goal) and defensive clearances.
6. Tackling: safely and fairly winning the ball from an opponent using the feet, timed correctly to avoid fouling.

PLAYER POSITIONS AND ROLES
- Goalkeeper: the only player allowed to handle the ball, but only within their own penalty area; responsible for preventing the opposing team from scoring.
- Defenders: players positioned mainly in their own half, responsible for stopping opposition attacks and regaining possession of the ball.
- Midfielders: players who link defence and attack, involved in both creating attacking opportunities and helping defend when possession is lost.
- Forwards/strikers: players positioned mainly in the opponent's half, primarily responsible for creating and finishing goal-scoring opportunities.

BASIC RULES
- A standard football match is played between two teams, each normally with a goalkeeper and outfield players (numbers may be adapted for younger/school-level games).
- A goal is scored when the whole of the ball crosses the goal line, between the goalposts and under the crossbar.
- Outfield players must not deliberately handle the ball with their hands or arms; only the goalkeeper may do so, and only inside their own penalty area.
- The game restarts with a kick-off at the start of each half and after a goal is scored.
- A throw-in is awarded to the opposing team when the ball fully crosses a touchline (sideline); it must be taken with both hands, from behind and over the head.
- A corner kick is awarded to the attacking team when the ball crosses the goal line (having last touched a defending player) without a goal being scored.
- A goal kick is awarded to the defending team when the ball crosses the goal line (having last touched an attacking player) without a goal being scored.

COMMON INFRINGEMENTS (FOULS)
- Handling the ball deliberately (by an outfield player).
- Dangerous or reckless tackling, such as tackling with excessive force, from behind, or with the studs raised toward an opponent.
- Pushing, holding, tripping or charging an opponent unfairly.
- Offside: broadly, an attacking player being in an 'illegal' position (nearer to the opponent's goal line than both the ball and the second-last defender) at the moment the ball is played to them, though offside rules can be simplified or adapted for younger learners.
A foul results in a free kick (direct or indirect, depending on the nature of the foul) or, for a foul committed by a defender inside their own penalty area, a penalty kick to the attacking team.

BASIC ATTACKING PRINCIPLES
- Creating and moving into space rather than standing still or bunching together with teammates.
- Passing quickly and accurately to keep possession and unbalance the defending team.
- Supporting the player with the ball by offering passing options at different angles and distances.
- Taking shooting opportunities when in a good position, rather than delaying unnecessarily.

BASIC DEFENDING PRINCIPLES
- Marking opposing players closely to limit their space and passing options.
- Pressuring the player in possession of the ball to force mistakes or slow down their attack.
- Covering teammates, staying in a position to help if a teammate is beaten by an attacker.
- Communicating with teammates to organise defensive positioning as a team.

SUMMARY
- Core football skills include dribbling, passing, receiving, shooting, heading and tackling.
- Positions (goalkeeper, defenders, midfielders, forwards) each have distinct roles in attack and defence.
- Basic rules govern scoring, restarts (kick-off, throw-in, corner kick, goal kick) and handball.
- Common fouls include handling, dangerous tackling and offside, resulting in free kicks or penalties.
- Good attacking relies on space and quick passing; good defending relies on marking, pressure, covering and communication.

GLOSSARY
Offside: a rule preventing an attacking player from gaining an unfair advantage by being in an illegal advanced position when the ball is played to them.
Penalty kick: a direct free kick awarded to the attacking team for a foul committed by the defending team inside their own penalty area.
Marking: staying close to an opponent to limit their space, passing options or scoring chances.
source: Adapted from the ZIMSEC/Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education Junior (Grade 3-7) Physical Education, Sport and Mass Displays Syllabus (2015-2022), Topic 5

subject: Physical Education
content:
TOPIC 5, SUBTOPIC B: NETBALL (Grade 7)

OBJECTIVES
Learners should be able to:
- demonstrate basic netball skills
- explain court areas and player positions in netball
- explain the basic rules and common infringements of netball
- apply basic attacking and defending principles in netball

BASIC SKILLS
1. Passing:
- Chest pass: the ball is held with both hands at chest height and pushed firmly and directly toward a teammate.
- Shoulder pass: a one-handed pass thrown from the shoulder, useful for longer or faster passes.
- Bounce pass: the ball is bounced once on the ground before reaching a teammate, useful for passing under an opponent's raised arms.
- Overhead pass: thrown from above the head, useful for passing over a defender who is close and low.
2. Catching: receiving the ball securely with both hands, fingers spread, absorbing the ball's speed by slightly 'giving' with the arms on catching.
3. Footwork: once a player catches the ball, whichever foot lands or is grounded first becomes the 'landing foot'; this foot cannot be lifted and re-grounded (dragged) while the player still holds the ball, though the player may pivot on it to change direction while keeping the other foot moving.
4. Shooting: performed only within the shooting circle by the Goal Shooter (GS) or Goal Attack (GA), using a controlled, arched shot aimed at the goal ring, with good balance and follow-through.
5. Dodging: quick changes of direction and speed used by a player without the ball to lose a defender and create space to receive a pass.

COURT AREAS AND PLAYER POSITIONS
A netball court is divided into thirds: two goal thirds (one at each end, each containing a shooting circle) and a centre third in the middle.
The seven playing positions, each restricted to specific areas of the court, are:
- Goal Shooter (GS): shoots for goals; allowed in the goal third (attacking) and shooting circle only.
- Goal Attack (GA): supports shooting and feeds the ball into the circle; allowed in the goal third (attacking), the shooting circle, and the centre third.
- Wing Attack (WA): feeds the ball to shooters; allowed in the centre third and the attacking goal third, but not inside the shooting circle.
- Centre (C): links defence and attack, allowed to move throughout the whole court except inside either shooting circle.
- Wing Defence (WD): marks the opposing Wing Attack; allowed in the centre third and the defending goal third, but not inside the shooting circle.
- Goal Defence (GD): marks the opposing Goal Attack; allowed in the goal third (defending), the shooting circle, and the centre third.
- Goal Keeper (GK): marks the opposing Goal Shooter and defends the goal; allowed in the goal third (defending) and shooting circle only.

BASIC RULES
- A goal is scored when the ball passes completely through the goal ring, and may only be shot from within the shooting circle by the GS or GA.
- Players may only move within the specific areas of the court permitted for their position.
- A player holding the ball must pass or shoot it within three seconds and may not run with it.
- Once a player lands with the ball, the landing foot cannot be lifted and re-grounded before releasing the ball (though pivoting on it is allowed).
- Contact, obstruction (standing too close, usually within 0.9m, to an opponent with the ball while attempting to intercept or defend) and pushing are not allowed.

COMMON INFRINGEMENTS
- Footwork error: dragging or stepping with the landing foot while holding the ball.
- Held ball: holding the ball for longer than three seconds without passing or shooting.
- Obstruction: defending too closely to an opponent without the correct distance, or raising arms in a way that unfairly blocks a pass or shot.
- Contact: unfairly pushing, bumping or leaning on another player.
- Offside: moving into an area of the court not permitted for your position.

BASIC ATTACKING AND DEFENDING PRINCIPLES
Attacking: moving into open space to offer a passing option, using dodges to lose a marking defender, and passing quickly and accurately to keep the ball moving forward.
Defending: marking an opponent closely (while respecting the correct defending distance to avoid obstruction), intercepting passes where possible, and recovering position quickly if beaten.

SUMMARY
- Core netball skills include the chest, shoulder, bounce and overhead passes, catching, correct footwork, shooting and dodging.
- The court is divided into thirds, with seven playing positions each restricted to specific playing areas.
- Basic rules govern shooting (circle only), footwork, held ball (three-second) limits, and fair contact.
- Common infringements include footwork errors, held ball, obstruction, contact and moving offside.
- Good attacking uses space and dodging; good defending uses correct marking distance and quick recovery.

GLOSSARY
Landing foot: the first foot grounded by a player after catching the ball, which cannot then be dragged or re-grounded while holding the ball.
Obstruction: illegally standing too close to or blocking an opponent while defending or intercepting.
Shooting circle: the marked semicircular area at each end of a netball court from within which shots at goal must be taken.
source: Adapted from the ZIMSEC/Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education Junior (Grade 3-7) Physical Education, Sport and Mass Displays Syllabus (2015-2022), Topic 5
